[Long reply right here] I worked on a fishing vessel for about four months. I had your same sentiment about the whole trip as well. The thing is this: I always felt recent generations have rarely been given a real chance to find their name. A real rite of passage. One filled with challenges that will break the weak and nurture the strongest. I'm talking about the way a village will kick out a boy at puberty with nothing to survive. If he can make it through the season/year/whatever in the distant woods/jungle using his knowledge to survive, than he returns to the village with a new name and is seen as a man. If he doesn't make it, it was for some reason we may never know, and everything moves on. Painfully and saddened by loss. Life gives and takes constantly. Going into an unfamiliar environment with the likelihood of dying is the important part. Knowing, not fearing, that at any point, death or serious injury WILL occur from lack of focus puts a person in the right state of mind. I think when in this frame of mind, not only is self preservation/will to live a motivation to keep moving positively forward, but also an important factor in keeping all your senses working at full power. Factor in going into a very secluded and overgrown natural environment, in all its chaotic beauty, this aids in the realization that the the only stimuli comes from what you see around yourself. Nature feeding on nature. Silence and individual nuances of natural noise. When you're by yourself in the middle of nowhere, living second to second, but completely accepting of demise, the natural environment gives you signs constantly. It just takes quieting the mind. Mental and physical fatigue are necessary to strengthen character, challenge personal thinking/beliefs, test reflexes, and most importantly, problem solving. These tests relax and strengthen the mind into reading/reflecting on EVERTHING in your immediate surroundings. That was working on the boat part. Backbreaking labor for 15-20 hours a day, for weeks at a time. Knowing absolutely nothing about Alaskan fishing. That was the immediate death environment. But on that boat, I experienced many moments of pure wonder out in the ocean. The life environment was the rain forest. Quiet and calm, but instant stealth everywhere. Pretty neat actually. I hiked as much as I could when on land. Usually sun up to sun down. Throughout the work, hiking and down time, I thought about what led me to that point. I was in my early twenties, single, kind of uncertain about where I was going in my life. Many forks in the road kind of thing. When the Alaska option popped up, I was certain this was the closest thing to a find/test myself/vision quest as I was going to encounter. The circumstances that put those options of going there in front of me felt terrifyingly amazing. Statistically, I figured I had zero chance of surviving. I'm 5'7, 115 soaking wet with boots. Yeah. Art school drop out from the city. Not much on the survival instincts. But for as much as I dismissed the idea of going when I first heard about it, something clicked. I had kind of wanted to someday explore rain forests and mountains. I figured if I die out there, so be it. It would be my own fault. No matter the circumstance. My trek there had a non existent return date, other than when season was over. My friends and family knew this. Most of them thought I was crazy and would not make it back. The few important ones had faith in me though. They knew this was my 'I need to do this for me' kind of thing. I actually told everyone that if I made it, I probably would just stay there for a few years. Or if I just came home after season was over, I'd try out being a fire jumper in the summer putting out forest fires. Either on the fishing vessel, or out hiking, I was completely comfortable with that place being my likely demise. Not that I wanted to die. On the contrary, I realized this trip would be the most amount of mental and physical stress I could ever put myself in. If I make it out with all my limbs and sanity mostly intact, then I can do anything. It would be the longest season of pure joy and hell and I walked away with a boat load of money. Took the year off to work on my portfolio, and just enjoyed life a lot more after that. No matter what I do, my experience finding myself in Alaska gave me more answers about myself and my place in the world than any other time in my life. In my thoughts, I asked the universe/whatever, many questions about what I had done and what I was doing. In that time, a lot of things happened, good and bad. I probably should've died multiple times out there. Lots of bad storms, breakdowns, random oh fuck shit just got real cuz we're sinking hundreds of miles away from anything kind of scenarios. The beauty in my opinion outweighed the pain. I had never seen so many natural wonders breathing all around me all the time. The mountains, ocean creatures, circle of life, etc., I still struggle to put into words. All the important questions I asked were always answered immediately by something in the natural environment. It was very surreal, but I knew I had to go at this with an open mind. Listening to what were signs of the universe replying to my thoughts became constant. My dreams out there on the ocean were some of the most psychedelic and introspective I had ever had, spanning my childhood, to my daily situation of life and death out on the ocean. I had a mantra of sorts my sister wrote to me before I left. I said it to myself every moment I awoke. It ends with "So be it". I had a similar mantra I would say to each fish I had to kill. If I was the last thing they were seeing before death, I'd want them to know that this was their current circle in life coming to an end. Their death would feed life, and one day I too will expire, be it in my sleep as an old man, or out in the ocean/woods. I too will be gutted and die. Metaphorically or literally, it doesn't matter to me. Fearing death is like panicking. Just a waste of time. I had to be willing and accepting of everything as a result of my own individual actions, no matter big or small. These types of inner journeying are what give you faith in self, action and though. As stated before, these treks make or break you. I don't feel college or the armed services provide that type of inner reflection needed to exercise all of ones capabilities, mentally and physically. That's not to say they don't. I'm sure they do for some and that's great. But I think these journeys should be predominantly solo. A few guides here and there are ok, but the journey is about the self not in competition with others, and knowing ones limitations. That can be harder to do in those settings. So yeah. I should stop now. Gotta water the garden. Sorry for the lengthy reply. As you can tell, I'm all for everyone finding their true selves. I'm just really partial to Alaska. It has a very special place in my heart.

I know not everyone will look kindly on this because of the subject matter, but I don't think that's a reason not to write it, as it is the truth as I understand it.

As a child, for some reason (that I still don't really know), I desired to die for the sake of the people I cared about. Or for the world itself. Like the heroes in the RPGs I would play as a kid. It wasn't just that life was depressing to me (I had no friends) to an extent. I have never found a reason for my extreme desire, but it was always there.

Growing up, I've always felt like God has been with me (I'm going somewhere with all of this). My mother being a Christian, she wanted me to go to Church from time to time (she didn't always make me go). Being who I am, the moment the preacher would tell you to read something in the Bible, I'd just keep reading and ignore the preacher from that point on. And reading the Bible, I felt that the presence I always felt with me was the God it spoke of. Same qualities.

As I grew older, I chose to be a Christian and follow the God I believed in. I learned more about what Jesus did for His people, and about what He wanted of us. That He cared about us and that He wanted things for us that were ultimately good.

After my parents died (dad when I was 12 and mom when I was 16), I lived with my step-dad for a while. I started to struggle with what God wanted of me. What surrender really is. And I came to the conclusion that it was death of selfishness, and that loving yourself isn't selfish.

And I realized that, based on my understanding, what God asks of those who follow Him is the death of who we were (in our sin), and life in who we would be in Him. As a Christian. Following His Word & such.

That's when it hit me. That Jesus died, then lived, for us. And He asks us to do the same for Him. To give Him what He wants (us). That that is the only thing we can give Him that is worth anything, and that that is all He wants.

And so, He made my dream come true and fulfilled my desire. That I should die for the sake of One I love. And added on that I should live for them too.

That is the deepest revelation I've ever had. I don't remember all of them, but that one definitely stuck with me.

If it's your deepest experience, it's your deepest experience. Who cares what Voat says. It's your life, your actions, and your decisions.

You aren't being manipulative, judgmental, or preachy. You're sharing an experience from your life that was incredible to you, and I am glad you did.
